title: Game Design with JavaScript
blurb: How games are designed and built: genres, look and feel, collision, hitboxes and hurtboxes, level design and game mechanics.
intro:
Making a game is half design (deciding what's fun, how it looks and feels, how levels teach the player) and half code (making things move, collide, score and get harder). This module does both.

You'll learn what makes a game a game, pick genres and art styles, add juice, then code movement, gravity, box and circle collision, walls, hitboxes and hurtboxes, invincibility frames, stomps, tile-based levels, difficulty curves, game states, combos and cooldowns. The boss stage is the heart of a real platformer.

Make your own game

Everything here also lives in the in the Sandbox: pick a starter game, add features with one click, press H to see the hitboxes, and change the code to make it yours.
links: MDN: Anatomy of a video game
MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design (paper)

stages.hook: Snake, Minecraft, chess and tag look nothing alike. So what do they have in common that a movie or a fireworks show doesn't?
stages.l:
Almost every game has the same four ingredients:

IngredientWhat it meansIn Snake
A goalSomething to aim forGet as long as you can
RulesWhat you can and can't doYou can't touch walls or your own tail
ChoicesDecisions that change what happensWhich way to turn, and when
FeedbackThe game shows you how you're doingThe snake grows and the score goes up

Take away the choices and it's a movie. Take away the goal and it's a toy (toys are great too, but they're not quite games).
stages.p: A student made an app where colorful fireworks explode on the screen forever. You can watch, but you can't do anything.
stages.q: Which ingredients is it missing to become a game?
opts: A goal and choices for the player
miss: Lots of great games have simple graphics. Pretty pictures don't make a game.
Music adds mood, but you still can't do anything.
More of the same is still just watching.
stages.why: With nothing to aim for and nothing to decide, it's a show. Add a goal (pop 20 fireworks before time runs out) and a choice (tap the ones you want), and it becomes a game.
stages.h: Look at the table. What can the viewer actually do, and what are they trying to achieve?

stages.l:
Game designers often use a model called MDA (from a 2004 paper by Hunicke, LeBlanc and Zubek):

  • Mechanics: the rules and actions written in code. Jump is 9 pixels high. Coins add 1 point.
  • Dynamics: what happens when players use those rules. Players learn to chain jumps across enemies.
  • Aesthetics: the feelings it creates. Tension, pride, surprise, being in control.

The designer builds mechanics and hopes for certain feelings. The player meets it the other way round: they feel first, and only later notice the rules. You only control the mechanics directly, so you tweak them until the feeling is right.
stages.p: In a game of tag, think about each statement.
opts: Whoever is It must touch another player
Players gang up near the safe zone and dodge together
The thrill of a narrow escape
miss: That's a rule, so it's a mechanic.
That's a feeling, so it's aesthetics.
That's a rule too, a mechanic.
stages.why: Nobody wrote a rule saying "gang up near the safe zone". It happens because of the rules. That's a dynamic: behavior that grows out of the mechanics.
stages.h: Mechanics are rules, aesthetics are feelings. Dynamics are what players end up doing because of the rules.

stages.l:
The core loop is the small set of actions players repeat over and over. If the core loop is fun, the game is fun. If it isn't, no amount of levels will fix it.

GameCore loop
MinecraftExplore → gather → craft → build → explore further
Pac-ManMove → eat dots → dodge ghosts → grab a power pellet → chase ghosts
Clicker gamesClick → earn → buy an upgrade → earn faster
Tip

Before making levels or art, make a tiny version of your core loop with plain boxes. If moving the boxes around is already fun, you're onto something.
stages.p: In a farming game, you plant seeds, wait for them to grow, harvest the crops, sell them, and buy better seeds.
stages.q: What is this game's core loop?
opts: Plant → grow → harvest → sell → buy better seeds
miss: The title screen happens once. A loop repeats.
Art and music matter a lot, but they aren't actions the player repeats.
An ending happens once, not over and over.
stages.why: That cycle is what players do again and again, and each lap leaves them a little stronger, which makes them want one more lap.
stages.h: A loop is something you repeat. Which answer describes actions that cycle back to the start?

stages.l:
A genre is a family of games that play in a similar way. Picking one tells you what players will expect.

GenreYou mostly...Examples
PlatformerRun and jump between platforms, seen from the sideMario, Celeste
Top-down adventureExplore a map from above, talk, fight, find itemsZelda, Pokémon
ShooterAim and fire at enemiesSpace Invaders, Splatoon
PuzzleFigure out a tricky problemTetris, Portal
RacingGet to the finish firstMario Kart
StrategyPlan ahead and manage resourcesChess, Clash Royale
RhythmPress buttons in time with musicBeat Saber, Guitar Hero
RoguelikeTry a new random run each time, starting over when you loseHades, Spelunky
stages.p: A student wants to make a game where each run makes a brand-new random dungeon, and if you die you start over from the beginning, a little wiser.
miss: There's no finish line to race to.
Nothing here is about timing to music.
Puzzles usually have one fixed solution. Here, the dungeon is random each time.
stages.why: Random levels plus starting over when you lose is exactly what roguelikes are about. Every run is different, so it stays fresh.
stages.h: Look for the genre with random runs and starting over.

stages.l:
The art style is how everything in your game looks: pixel art, flat shapes, hand-drawn, cartoon, low-poly 3D. Simple styles are great for small teams. What matters most is that everything matches: the same level of detail, the same outlines, the same palette.

A good trick is to pick a small palette of 4 to 8 colors and use only those. Limits make games look planned instead of thrown together.
stages.p: This screenshot mixes a photo-like background, a pixel-art hero and a smooth cartoon coin.
opts: The styles don't match, so nothing feels like it belongs together
miss: Size isn't the issue here.
Even more colors would make it messier.
A story won't fix how it looks.
stages.why: Three different styles fight each other. Choose one style and one small palette, and use it for the hero, the coins, the background and even the score font.
stages.h: Look at how each object is drawn. Do they look like they come from the same game?

stages.l:
In a fast game, players don't have time to read. Color does the talking:

  • The player should stand out from everything else, often with the brightest color.
  • Danger is usually warm and loud: red, orange, spiky shapes.
  • Good stuff (coins, health) is shiny or soft: gold, green, round shapes.
  • The background is darker or duller, so it never competes.
Tip

Squint at a screenshot. You should still be able to find the player, the danger and the goal. Pair color with shape too, so color-blind players can tell them apart.
stages.p: Here's a level from a student's game.
stages.q: Why do players keep losing track of their character?
stages.html: Lives 3
opts: The player is almost the same color as the background
miss: Red for danger is a good choice.
Round, shiny pickups are a good choice.
The floor is fine. Look for the hero.
stages.why: Teal on teal disappears. Give the player a color nothing else uses, like bright white or yellow, and they'll never lose sight of it.
stages.h: Can you even find the player? It's at the left.

stages.l:
Game feel is how good it is to just move and act. Designers add juice: small effects that make every action feel strong. The term was popularised by Martin Jonasson and Petri Purho.

  • Particles: sparkles when you grab a coin, dust when you land.
  • Screen shake: a quick wobble when something big happens.
  • Sound: a satisfying blip for every pickup.
  • Squash and stretch: the hero squishes when landing and stretches when jumping.
  • Hit pause: the game freezes for a few frames when a big hit lands.

Good feedback comes instantly, within about a tenth of a second, and is sized to the event: tiny for a coin, big for a boss.
stages.p: Players say defeating enemies in a student's game feels flat. The enemy just vanishes.
stages.q: Which change adds the most juice?
opts: Add a burst of particles, a short shake and a sound when an enemy is defeated
Make the enemy disappear more slowly over 5 seconds
miss: More health makes fights longer, not more satisfying.
A menu doesn't change how a hit feels.
Five seconds is far too slow. Feedback should be instant.
stages.why: Several small effects at once, all within a fraction of a second, make the hit feel powerful. Nothing about the rules changed, only the feedback.
stages.h: Juice is extra feedback, not extra rules.

stages.p: A boss in a student's game does a huge slam attack with no warning. Players say it feels cheap.
opts: Give the boss a clear wind-up first, like raising its arms and flashing, before it slams
miss: A weak surprise attack still feels unfair.
Bosses are fun when they're fair, so keep it.
More lives hides the problem but doesn't fix it.
stages.why: A warning before an attack is called a telegraph. When players can see it coming, getting hit feels like their mistake, and dodging it feels great. Fair danger is fun danger.
stages.h: Players don't mind dying when they could have seen it coming.

stages.hook: Time to build. Every 2D game, from Pong to Celeste, starts by drawing rectangles on a canvas.
stages.l:
A <canvas> is a grid of pixels you can draw on. You draw with its context, usually called ctx. In these stages (and in the Game Studio), canvas and ctx are already set up for you. The top-left corner is (0, 0). x goes right and y goes down, which is upside down compared to math class.

ctx.fillStyle = "skyblue";          // pick a color
ctx.fillRect(10, 20, 50, 30);        // x, y, width, height

Things you draw later go on top of things drawn earlier, so draw the background first.
stages.p: On the 320 by 180 canvas: fill the whole thing with #1b1f3a (dark blue). Then draw the ground: a #5c6a99 rectangle at x 0, y 160, 320 wide and 20 tall. Then draw the player: a #4cc9f0 square at x 40, y 136, size 24.
stages.h: Three pairs of lines: set ctx.fillStyle, then call ctx.fillRect(x, y, w, h). Background first, then ground, then player.
stages.st: // 1. background  2. ground  3. player

stages.hook: Games look smooth, but nothing really moves. The game redraws the screen about 60 times a second, and each time the player is drawn a little further along.
stages.l: Each redraw is called a frame. Movement is just adding the speed to the position once per frame.
stages.p: This simulates 3 frames. What does it print?
opts:
frame 1: x = 14
frame 2: x = 18
frame 3: x = 22

frame 1: x = 10
frame 2: x = 14
frame 3: x = 18

frame 1: x = 4
frame 2: x = 8
frame 3: x = 12
miss: The speed is added before printing, so frame 1 already shows 14.
x starts at 10, not 0.
console.log runs on every pass of the loop, not just the last one.
stages.why: Each frame adds 4 to x: 10 becomes 14, 18, then 22. At 60 frames a second, a speed of 4 means 240 pixels every second.
stages.h: Add 4 to x, print, and repeat three times. Start from 10.

stages.l:
Most games keep a keys object that says which keys are held down right now. Each frame, the game checks it and moves the player.

function fly(bird, keys) {
  if (keys.space) bird.y -= 5;   // up means a smaller y!
  return bird;
}

Remember: on screen, up is minus y and down is plus y.
stages.p: Write move(p, keys). p has x, y and speed. keys has true or false for left, right, up and down. Change p.x and p.y by p.speed for each held key, then return p.
stages.h: Four separate ifs (not else-ifs, so diagonals work). Left subtracts from x, right adds, up subtracts from y, down adds.

stages.l:
Without limits, players walk right off the edge of the world. The fix is called clamping: if a number goes past a limit, snap it back to the limit.

Math.max(0, -12)    // 0   (picks the bigger one)
Math.min(100, 140)  // 100 (picks the smaller one)

For a player 24 pixels wide on a 480-wide screen, x must stay between 0 and 480 - 24 = 456.
stages.p: Write clamp(value, min, max) that returns value, but never less than min and never more than max.
stages.h: Combine them: one call stops it going too low, the other stops it going too high. You can nest one inside the other.

stages.l:
Gravity isn't a speed, it's a change in speed. Every frame, gravity adds a little to the falling speed vy (v for velocity), then vy is added to y. That's why falls start slow and get faster.

ball.vx += wind;    // wind changes the speed
ball.x += ball.vx;  // the speed changes the position

When the player reaches the floor, it should stop: put it exactly on the floor and set vy back to 0.
stages.p: Write fall(p) for one frame. Add 0.5 to p.vy, then add p.vy to p.y. If p.y is now more than 300 (the floor), set p.y to 300 and p.vy to 0. Return p.
stages.h: Speed first, then position, then the floor check with an if.

stages.l:
A jump is just setting vy to a big negative number. Gravity does the rest, slowing the rise and pulling the player back down.

But you can only jump from the ground. Here's a pro trick called coyote time (named after the cartoon coyote who runs off cliffs): let players jump for a few frames after walking off a ledge. Players press jump a moment too late all the time, and this forgives them. Players rarely notice it, but games without it feel unfair.

// p.onGround: is the player standing on something?
// p.airFrames: how many frames since it last stood on something
stages.p: Write canJump(p). Return true if p.onGround is true, or if p.airFrames is less than 6 (coyote time). Otherwise return false.
stages.h: One return with || between the two conditions.

stages.hook: How does a game know a sword hit a slime, or Mario landed on a Goomba? Checking every pixel of every picture 60 times a second would be far too slow.
stages.l:
Instead, games wrap things in invisible simple shapes, usually boxes or circles, and only check whether the shapes touch. This is called collision detection.

The boxes don't have to match the picture exactly. Designers make them a little smaller than the player's sprite, so near misses count as misses. Players think "phew, close one!" instead of "that didn't touch me!"
stages.p: Players complain they keep dying when a spike only looks like it brushed past their hair.
stages.html: dashed line = the player's collision box
opts: Make the player's box a bit smaller than the picture
Make the box even bigger to be safe
miss: A bigger box makes the problem worse: even more hits that don't look like hits.
Spikes are good challenge. They just need fair boxes.
Pixel checks are slow and still feel harsh at the edges.
stages.why: The box sticks out past the picture, so the spike "hits" empty air. Shrinking the box a little makes collisions match what players see, and close calls feel exciting instead of unfair.
stages.h: Compare the dashed box with the blue body. Which one does the spike actually touch?

stages.l:
The simplest collision: is a point inside a box? You need this for clicking buttons, mouse aiming, and bullets that are just a dot.

A box r has x, y (its top-left corner), w and h. A point is inside when it's between the left and right edges and between the top and bottom edges.

// is a number between two others?
const inRange = n >= low && n <= high;
stages.p: Write pointIn(px, py, r) that returns true if the point is inside box r (edges count as inside) and false otherwise.
stages.h: The right edge is at r.x + r.w and the bottom edge at r.y + r.h. You need four comparisons joined with &&.

stages.hook: Two boxes overlap when they overlap left-to-right AND top-to-bottom. If there's a gap on either axis, they're apart. This test is called AABB (axis-aligned bounding boxes), and almost every 2D game uses it.
stages.l: On one axis, A and B overlap when A's left edge is before B's right edge, and A's right edge is after B's left edge.
stages.p: What does this print?
miss: A ends at 30 and B starts at 25, so they share 25 to 30.
A ends at 30 but C doesn't start until 40, so there's a gap.
A and B share the stretch from 25 to 30.
stages.why: A (10 to 30) and B (25 to 45) share 25 to 30, so they overlap. A and C have a gap from 30 to 40, so they don't. Do the same check on y as well, and you have full box collision.
stages.h: Draw the three ranges on a number line from 0 to 50.

stages.l:
Now both axes at once. Two boxes touch when all four of these are true:

CheckMeaning
a.x < b.x + b.wA's left edge is before B's right edge
a.x + a.w > b.xA's right edge is after B's left edge
(same for y and h)A's top is above B's bottom, and A's bottom is below B's top
Tip

If boxes only touch edge to edge, like a player standing exactly on the floor, this counts as not overlapping. That's what you want, or players would get stuck in every floor.
stages.p: Write overlaps(a, b) for two boxes with x, y, w and h. Return true when they overlap.
stages.h: Copy the two x checks from the table, then write the two matching checks using y and h. Join all four with &&.

stages.l: Here's how almost every game picks things up: check each coin against the player, and for each one touching, count it and remove it. filter keeps only the coins that weren't touched. In this game, positions are the centers of things, and a coin counts as touched when it's less than 16 pixels away on both x and y.
stages.p: Tap the lines into order so collect(player, coins) returns how many coins the player touched and the coins that are left.
stages.h: Start the count at 0, then filter. Inside the filter, work out whether this coin is touching, and an if handles touched coins. Return the count and the remaining coins together at the end.

stages.t: Bug hunt: stuck in the floor
stages.l: A student's player keeps getting stuck: it stands on the floor, but the game thinks it's inside the floor, so it can't walk.
stages.p: This overlaps says a box sitting exactly on top of the floor is overlapping it. Fix it so boxes that only touch edge to edge do not count.
stages.h: Look at the comparison signs. Should touching edges (equal values) count?

stages.l:
Balls, bubbles and planets fit circles better than boxes. Two circles touch when the distance between their centers is less than their two radiuses added together.

// distance between two points (Pythagoras)
const d = Math.hypot(x2 - x1, y2 - y1);
console.log(Math.hypot(3, 4)); // 5
stages.p: Write circlesHit(a, b). Each circle has x, y (its center) and r (radius). Return true if the distance between centers is less than a.r + b.r.
stages.h: Work out the distance with Math.hypot(b.x - a.x, b.y - a.y), then compare it with the two radiuses added together.

stages.l:
Detecting a collision isn't enough. For walls, you have to push the player back out. The standard way:

  1. Move the player on x only.
  2. If it now overlaps a wall: moving right means put its right edge on the wall's left edge (p.x = wall.x - p.w). Moving left means put its left edge on the wall's right edge (p.x = wall.x + wall.w).
  3. Then do the same for y separately.

Doing the axes one at a time is what lets players slide smoothly along walls.
stages.p: Write moveX(p, dx, walls): add dx to p.x, then push p out of any wall it overlaps, as above. Return p.x. overlaps is already in the starter.
stages.h: After p.x += dx, loop with for (const wall of walls). Inside, if they overlap, use dx > 0 to choose which side to snap to.

stages.l:
Action games give characters several boxes, each with its own job:

BoxJobUsually drawn as
HurtboxWhere you can be hit. Your body.Green
HitboxWhere your attack hits. A sword swing, a punch, a bullet. Usually only there while the attack is active.Red or yellow
Collision box (pushbox)Stops you walking through walls and other characters.Blue

An attack lands when an attacker's hitbox overlaps a defender's hurtbox. Fighting games like Street Fighter move these boxes every frame to match the animation, so a kick's hitbox only reaches out while the leg is out.
stages.p: Here's a knight swinging a sword at a slime, with debug boxes turned on.
stages.html:
A
B
C
miss: A is the knight's hurtbox: where the knight can get hit.
C is the slime's hurtbox: where the slime can get hit.
stages.why: B is the hitbox. It only exists while the sword swings. If B overlaps the slime's hurtbox C, the slime takes damage. Notice that B doesn't touch C yet, so this swing would miss.
stages.h: Hitbox = what hits. Which box belongs to the weapon?

stages.l:
An attack has a hitbox and an active flag (true only during the frames where the swing can hurt). A target has a hurtbox. The attack lands only when it's active and the boxes overlap.

// a box inside an object is just another object
const sword = { active: true, hitbox: { x: 100, y: 92, w: 62, h: 24 } };
console.log(sword.hitbox.w); // 62
stages.p: Write attackLands(attack, target) that returns true only if attack.active is true and attack.hitbox overlaps target.hurtbox. overlaps is in the starter.
stages.h: Combine attack.active and a call to overlaps(...) with &&.

stages.l:
Without protection, touching an enemy for one second would take 60 lives, one per frame! So after getting hurt, the player gets invincibility frames (i-frames): a short time where its hurtbox is switched off. Most games make the player blink during i-frames so you can see it.

// counting down a timer each frame
if (shield.timer > 0) shield.timer--;
stages.p: Write takeHit(p). If p.iframes is more than 0, nothing happens. Otherwise take 1 from p.hp and set p.iframes to 60. Return p either way.
stages.h: One if checking p.iframes === 0 (or <= 0) with two lines inside, then return p.

stages.l:
In Mario, touching a Goomba from the side hurts you, but landing on its head defeats it. Same overlap, different result! The game checks which way you were moving:

  • The player must be falling (vy > 0).
  • Last frame, the player's feet were above the enemy's top. Last frame's bottom edge is p.y + p.h - p.vy.
stages.p: Write stompOrHurt(p, enemy) for a player that is already overlapping the enemy. Return "stomp" if p.vy > 0 and last frame's bottom (p.y + p.h - p.vy) was at or above enemy.y. Otherwise return "hurt".
stages.h: Store last frame's bottom in a variable first. Then one if with && and <=.

stages.l:
Pro developers add a debug view that draws every box, so they can see exactly why something did or didn't hit. strokeRect draws just the outline of a rectangle.

ctx.strokeStyle = "white";
ctx.lineWidth = 2;
ctx.strokeRect(5, 5, 40, 40);
stages.p: Draw an outline for every box in boxes with lineWidth 2. Hurtboxes (kind is "hurt") are green #57f287, and hitboxes (kind is "hit") are red #ff3b5c.
stages.h: Loop over boxes. Pick the color with b.kind === "hit" ? ... : ..., set it as ctx.strokeStyle, then call strokeRect.

stages.hook: The first level of Super Mario Bros. has no tutorial text, yet millions of people learned to play from it. How?
stages.l:
Nintendo's designers often build each level in four beats. Super Mario 3D World's director, Koichi Hayashida, compared it to kishōtenketsu, a four-part way of telling stories:

  1. Introduce one new idea somewhere safe, where failing costs almost nothing. A moving platform over solid ground.
  2. Develop it: the same idea, a little harder. Now the platform is over a pit.
  3. Twist it: combine it with something else, or turn it upside down. Now enemies ride the platforms.
  4. Conclude: one last test that uses everything, then a reward.
Tip

One new idea per level is plenty. Players remember a level by its idea: the windy level, the ice level, the level where the floor falls.
stages.p: A student's level introduces bouncy mushrooms. Here are four sections, out of order.
opts: Bouncing across mushrooms over a long pit
One mushroom on flat ground, with a coin above it
Bouncing on mushrooms while dodging cannonballs
A tricky final run of mushrooms leading to the flag
miss: That's develop: the same idea with real danger.
That's the twist: mushrooms combined with something new.
That's the conclusion that tests everything.
stages.why: A single mushroom on safe ground lets players try it with nothing to lose, and the coin above it quietly says "jump on this". That's teaching without any text.
stages.h: Where can a player try the new thing without any risk?

stages.l:
Players have the most fun when the challenge is just a bit above their skill. Too easy is boring, too hard is frustrating. Psychologists call the happy middle flow.

Since players get better as they play, the challenge should rise too. But not in a straight line: good games go up in a sawtooth, with a hard part followed by a short breather, like a calm room with a save point after a boss.

Too easyFlowToo hard
BoredFocused, "one more try"Frustrated, quits
stages.p: Testers of a student's game play level 1 and 2 happily. Most quit during level 3.
opts: Level 3 is a big jump in difficulty instead of a step
miss: More levels won't help if players quit at level 3.
They enjoyed level 1, so it's not that.
Music rarely makes people quit in one specific level.
stages.why: When everyone quits at the same spot, that spot is a difficulty spike. Split it into smaller steps, or teach the new skill earlier, so the curve rises smoothly.
stages.h: Everyone quits at the same place. What's different about that place?

stages.l:
Good levels lead players without signs saying "go here". Designers use:

  • Breadcrumbs: a trail of coins showing the path, or the jump to make.
  • Light and color: the exit glows, important doors are a different color.
  • Landmarks: a big tower you can see from anywhere.
  • Risk and reward: a shortcut over spikes with extra coins. Brave players take it, careful players don't have to.
stages.p: Testers keep missing a secret area above the start of a level.
stages.q: What's the gentlest way to hint at it?
stages.html: The secret ledge is up top. Nothing points to it.
opts: A big sign saying SECRET HERE
A short trail of coins leading up toward the ledge
miss: A sign ruins the surprise. Secrets feel best when players work them out.
Invisible makes it even harder to find.
Secrets are a great reward for curious players. Keep it, just hint at it.
stages.why: Coins are a breadcrumb trail. Players already love collecting them, so a trail that leads upward pulls them toward the secret, and finding it feels like their own discovery.
stages.h: What do players already chase without being told?

stages.l:
Many games store levels as text. Each character is a tile, so you can design levels in a text editor without changing any code:

const LEVEL = [
  "     o   ",
  "  ####   ",
  "P      e ",
  "#########"
];
console.log(LEVEL[2][0]); // "P"   (row 2, column 0)

The row number is y and the position in the string is x. map[y][x] gets one tile.
stages.p: Write findTiles(map, ch) that returns an array of [x, y] pairs for every tile in map that equals ch, going row by row, left to right.
stages.h: Two loops: the outer one over the rows (y), the inner one over the characters in that row (x). When map[y][x] === ch, push [x, y].

stages.t: What tile am I standing on?
stages.l:
With a tile map, collision gets easy: turn a pixel position into a tile position by dividing by the tile size and rounding down.

const size = 16;
console.log(Math.floor(40 / size)); // 2  (pixel 40 is in tile 2)

Outside the map, treat it as a wall ("#"), so nothing can wander off the edge of the world.
stages.p: Write tileAt(map, px, py, size) that returns the character of the tile at pixel (px, py). If the tile is outside the map, return "#".
stages.h: Work out tx and ty with Math.floor. If ty is below 0 or past the last row, or tx is below 0 or past the end of the row, return "#".

stages.l:
Endless games get harder over time by spawning enemies more often. A smooth way: start with a long gap between spawns, shrink it a bit every few seconds, and stop at a minimum so it never becomes impossible.

// every 600 frames (10 seconds), level goes up by 1
const level = Math.floor(frame / 600);
stages.p: Write spawnDelay(frame). Start at 60 frames between spawns. Every 300 frames, it gets 5 shorter. It never goes below 15.
stages.h: Count the steps with Math.floor(frame / 300), take 5 times that from 60, and use Math.max so it can't go under 15.

stages.l:
A game is always in one state: the title screen, playing, paused, or game over. Each state reacts to different things. This is called a state machine, and it keeps the code tidy: pressing P on the title screen shouldn't pause anything.

StateEventNew state
titlestartplay
playpausepaused
pausedpauseplay
playdieover
overstartplay

Any other combination leaves the state as it is.
stages.p: Write nextState(state, event) that follows the table and returns the new state. For anything not in the table, return state unchanged.
stages.h: A chain of ifs works, checking both the state and the event each time. Or use a switch on the state.

stages.l:
A combo rewards doing well several times in a row. It's a classic mechanic that creates a great dynamic: players take more risks to keep the streak going.

A common rule: every 5 hits in a row adds 1 to a multiplier, up to a cap.

const bonus = Math.min(1 + Math.floor(streak / 10), 3);
stages.p: Write comboPoints(combo). A hit is worth 10 points times a multiplier. The multiplier is 1 + Math.floor(combo / 5), but never more than 4.
stages.h: Work out the multiplier with Math.min(..., 4), then return 10 times it.

stages.l: If holding Space fired 60 bullets a second, shooters would be no challenge at all. A cooldown is a wait between uses. It's also a great balancing tool: strong moves get long cooldowns.
stages.p: Write canUse(now, lastUsed, cooldown) that returns true if at least cooldown frames have passed since lastUsed. Something never used yet has lastUsed set to a big negative number like -9999, so it's always ready.
stages.h: The time passed is now - lastUsed. Compare it with the cooldown using >=.

stages.p: A student playtests their platformer. Their notes say: "Jumping feels floaty and slow. Enemies hit me from far away. Level 2 is way harder than level 1. Nothing happens when I grab a coin."
opts: Add a story, a menu and more levels
Stronger gravity and jump, smaller enemy hitboxes, a gentler step to level 2, and a sparkle and sound on coins
Make the game slower so there's more time to react
miss: None of those touch the four problems the testers found.
Slower makes floaty jumps feel even worse.
Lots of lives hides the problems instead of fixing them.
stages.why: Each note maps to one thing you learned: game feel (gravity and jump strength), fair hitboxes, the difficulty curve, and juice. That's how real designers work: playtest, write down what feels wrong, tweak, and test again.
stages.h: Look for the answer that fixes all four notes, one by one.

stages.t: Boss: one frame of a platformer
stages.l: Every game is one function run 60 times a second. Time to write it. Everything you need is in this module: movement, gravity, the floor, collecting, hurtboxes and i-frames. When you're done, open the and build a real, playable game around these same ideas.
stages.p:
Write tick(g) for one frame. g has p (the player: x, y, w, h, vy, iframes), keys, coins, enemies, score and lives.

  1. If g.keys.left, take 3 from p.x. If g.keys.right, add 3.
  2. Gravity: add 0.5 to p.vy, then add p.vy to p.y.
  3. Floor: if p.y + p.h is more than 300, set p.y to 300 - p.h and p.vy to 0.
  4. If p.iframes is more than 0, take 1 from it.
  5. Remove every coin that overlaps the player, adding 1 to g.score for each.
  6. If any enemy overlaps the player and p.iframes is 0, take 1 from g.lives and set p.iframes to 60.

Return g. overlaps is in the starter.
stages.h: Do the steps in order. For coins, g.coins = g.coins.filter(c => ...) where the filter adds to the score and returns false for touched coins. For enemies, g.enemies.some(e => overlaps(p, e)) tells you if any touch.
